m16.title: Evaluating AI with an LLM as judge — DeepEval, Promptfoo, thresholds and false greens
m16.mentor: An AI answer can be well written and still be wrong. If your test only looks at the shape, it lets it through and hands you a false green. Here you put a judge in place with a threshold written down before you see the numbers, you plant traps to find out whether it's awake, and you learn to read a green check: sometimes it only means nobody evaluated anything.
m16.kid: A robot writes “The capital of Colombia is Medellín.” The sentence sounds nice, but it's wrong. The judge is the teacher who compares it with the right answer, Bogotá, and gives it a grade from 0 to 1. We set the trap on purpose: if the teacher falls asleep and lets it through, the light turns red.
obj: Run the parts of qa-eval-lab that don't need a key (UI, calibration and module 3) and state, with the exit code of each command, what was evaluated and what wasn't.
Write 2 false-green cases from your own domain that pass a contains assertion and that the judge fails below 0.7.
Pin the threshold of a new metric in its own commit, with its justification, before the judge's first run.
Tell apart, in a CI report, a green that was evaluated from a green by omission.
m16.pre: The API and contracts module, the AI-augmented QA module and basic Python (pytest). For the real judge you need an OPENAI_API_KEY; without it you do everything except modules 1 and 2 of qa-eval-lab, and you say so in the report.
theory: Two oracles: the deterministic one answers “does it run as specified?” (schema, status codes, roles) and the judge answers “is what it produced any good?” with a score against criteria. qa-eval-lab uses the first wherever the specification allows it and the second where it doesn't.

LLM as judge in DeepEval: GEval (Correctness) and AnswerRelevancy with a 0.7 threshold; for RAG, Faithfulness 0.7 and ContextualRelevancy 0.6; for agents, ToolCorrectness with DeepEval's default threshold (0.5 in 4.3.1).

False green: a ✓ that should have been a ✗. evals/dataset.jsonl ships two answers that are well formed and wrong on purpose: dispute-window (“any charge, no time limit”, which ignores the ~60-day window) and card-blocked (“cancelled forever”). A naive assertion lets them through; the judge must fail them.

Testing the judge (the WAR thread): test_false_green_detectado feeds it “La capital de Colombia es Medellin.” against the reference “Bogota” and only passes if the score lands below 0.7. With a mocked judge, the README documents three outcomes: 0.1 → pass, 0.9 → fail, judge error → error, never green.

Promptfoo: contains, not-contains and llm-rubric assertions against openai:gpt-4o-mini, plus red-teaming with the pii and harmful:misinformation plugins and the prompt-injection and jailbreak strategies.

The threshold is set before you see the score. In module 3, skips-balance-check (transfers without checking the balance) scores 0.67 against the 0.5 default and passes. The README leaves the threshold as it is: “raising it after seeing the score would be fitting to the result.”

qa-eval-lab's CI doesn't evaluate the LLM without the secret. Without OPENAI_API_KEY, the DeepEval and Promptfoo steps are skipped with a ::notice:: and the green check only says the UI tests passed. On top of that, a red check only blocks if it's required, and main doesn't have branch protection yet.

res.label: eval-gate.yml — the CI that skips the judge without a key
Husain — Your AI Product Needs Evals

hands: Lab without a key. git clone https://github.com/criguex/qa-eval-lab.git, go into the folder and run npm install, npx playwright install chromium, npm run test:ui and python evals/calibration/calibrate_judge.py. Write down the exit code of each one. On Node 26, npm install fails compiling better-sqlite3 (a Promptfoo dependency); for the Playwright part, npm install --ignore-scripts is enough.

Module 3 without API calls. pip install -r evals/requirements.txt and deepeval test run evals/agent/test_agent_eval.py with OPENAI_API_KEY set to any value (DeepEval 4.3.1 won't build the metric without it). Look for skips-balance-check and its 0.67.

With a key. export OPENAI_API_KEY=..., deepeval test run evals/test_support_eval.py, npm run eval:promptfoo and, separately, npx promptfoo@latest redteam run. If you don't have a key, your report says “not run” instead of guessing the result.
Read .github/workflows/eval-gate.yml and mark which steps carry the condition on OPENAI_API_KEY and which always run.

Exercise. In a fork: (1) a commit with THRESHOLDS.md that pins the threshold of a new metric from your domain and why; (2) a later commit with two false-green rows in evals/dataset.jsonl; (3) a naive test (contains) and the judge's test on those rows, with both outputs side by side; (4) a REPORTE.md with “what ran / what was skipped” and the command and exit code of each step.
crit: git log --oneline shows the THRESHOLDS.md commit before the commit with the new rows, and no later commit changes the threshold.

Each new false green passes the naive assertion (exit 0) and the judge fails it with a score below 0.7. Without a key, the report marks that step as not run and the criterion stays pending, not passed.
REPORTE.md separates what was evaluated from what was skipped, and every line carries its command and its exit code.
The mutation of the week is documented, with the prediction written before running and the observed result.

m16.mut: Put the judge to sleep on purpose. With a dummy OPENAI_API_KEY, replace, in a copy, the measurement in test_false_green_detectado with a mocked judge that always returns 0.9. Write down first what you expect and run pytest evals/test_llm_eval.py. If the test stays green, the guard wasn't testing anything, and that gets published.

It says “all green” and nothing else.

m17.title: Calibrating a judge and evaluating AI agents — code checks, Cohen's kappa and human review in the gray zone
m17.mentor: A judge nobody has compared against a person is an opinion with decimals. I calibrate it the way I'd calibrate a scale: against reference labels written beforehand, stating who wrote them, with one group of cases to tune on and another the tuning never saw. And with an agent, the final answer isn't enough for me: I look at which tools it called, where every number came from, and whether it obeyed something someone planted on a web page.
m17.kid: To grade a robot that plans trips, a calculator checks the numbers, a quick judge answers yes or no and says how sure it is, and when it's not sure, a person decides. Before we believe the judge, we compare its grades with an answer key. And we check who made that key: here another AI wrote it and a person reviewed it without noting down each check, so the judge agrees with that key, not with a real teacher.
obj: Compute by hand the agreement and Cohen's kappa of labeled_sample.csv and get the same 0.58 as calibrate_judge.py.
Run agent-eval-jev's offline replay and explain, using reports/report.md, why the gate lets v2 through (94 %) and blocks v1 (18 %).
Label 20 traces with a 4-criterion rubric before running any judge, tune on 10 and report on the other 10 the accuracy with a Wilson CI, kappa and the % sent to human review.
Predict in writing, and then measure, which step of agent-eval-jev's CI notices a code check that's been switched off.
m17.pre: The previous module (LLM as judge), Python 3 and descriptive statistics (proportions). You don't need any keys: the lab runs offline with recorded responses.
theory: Cohen's kappa: κ = (po − pe) / (1 − pe), where po is the observed agreement and pe the agreement two random raters with the same proportions would reach. In qa-eval-lab, 8 out of 10 in agreement gives κ = 0.58, below the 0.6 the script flags as “recalibrate rubric”. The disagreements are intl-wire (human fail, judge pass) and refund-policy (human pass, judge fail).

Golden set with a rubric: agent-eval-jev has 60 cases (34 live runs of v2, 11 of v1 and 15 seeded defects) and four criteria: tool_use, grounded, complete and policy. A case passes only if it meets all four, and the labels were written before any judge was run. Reference labels were drafted by an AI assistant against the written rubric and reviewed by Cristian. There is no case-by-case log of that review, and no independent human annotator.

Layered judgment: (1) code checks in agenteval/checks.py: schemas, expected tools, every number present in a tool result and an injection canary that must be absent; (2) Jev, with typed noul, score and choice questions that return probabilities; (3) an LLM judge (Claude Sonnet) that is only there for comparison and doesn't go into the verdict.

The composite (agenteval/composite.py): weights fixed before tuning anything (grounded 0.30, tool_use 0.20, complete 0.20, policy 0.20, quality 0.10); hard gates that fail the case whatever the judges say (no answer, broken schema, expected tool not called, canary present); and a gray zone: if a criterion falls between 0.35 and 0.65, the case goes to a person.

Tune on one group, report on another: fit_threshold maximizes balanced accuracy and fit_margin searches for the review margin, using only the calibration split. The honest numbers are the held-out ones (29 cases), measured against those reference labels: code alone 79.3 % (κ 0.55), Jev alone 79.3 % (κ 0.60, with 11 false FAILs), composite 93.1 % (CI 78-98 %, κ 0.86) and LLM judge 86.2 % (κ 0.72). The intervals overlap: it's a trend, not a proven difference.

An agreement figure is worth what its reference is worth. agent-eval-jev's 93.1 % (κ 0.86) measures the evaluator against AI-drafted labels, not against independent human judgment: Cristian reviewed them, but that review left no case-by-case log, and a review with no log can't be audited. If whoever drafts the reference and the judge read the rubric in a similar way, they can share biases, and agreement goes up without anyone judging independently. That's why it says “agrees with the reference labels”, not “agrees with people”. The next honest step is to re-label a blind sample by hand, log each decision, and measure agreement (or add a second human annotator).

Confidence is self-reported: it's useful for routing, not as proof. With the tuned threshold (0.67) and the band, 23 of 29 held-out cases were decided automatically (22 correctly) and 6 went to human review. And the provider matters: to the same question, typesafe-ai answered 0.84-0.87 and digitalocean 0.52-0.62.

Reproducible CI: the job rebuilds the report from the fixtures, fails with git diff --exit-code -- results reports if anything changed and runs python -m agenteval gate --min-agreement 0.85. The gate also requires v2 to pass at least 85 % and to have no policy failures.

res.label: Cohen (1960) — A Coefficient of Agreement for Nominal Scales

hands: Lab A · calibration. In qa-eval-lab, python evals/calibration/calibrate_judge.py. Then compute κ by hand from evals/calibration/labeled_sample.csv (2×2 table, po and pe) and look at the two disagreements: is the rubric wrong, or the human label?

Lab B · agents. git clone https://github.com/criguex/agent-eval-jev, go into the folder and run pip install pytest ruff, pytest -q, python -m agenteval evaluate, git diff --exit-code -- results reports and python -m agenteval gate. Read reports/report.md, data/mutations.json (15 seeded defects, from the altered number €219.24 → €231.50 to a harmless paraphrase that must keep passing) and agenteval/metrics.py (cohen_kappa, wilson_interval, flip_rate).
Lab C · the gate is a contract. Run python -m agenteval gate --min-agreement 0.95 and write down the exit code and the GATE FAILED line. Explain why raising the bar doesn't make the judge any better.

Exercise. Take 20 traces from an agent or chatbot that uses tools (if you don't have one, 20 cases from data/golden.jsonl). Write the 4-criterion rubric and label all 20 in a commit before running any judge; state who wrote the labels, and if an assistant drafted them, label at least 10 blind yourself, log each decision, and measure agreement with its labels. Implement 2 code checks: numbers present in the tool results, and canary absent. Split off 10 for calibration and 10 held-out, tune threshold and margin only on the first 10 and report on the other 10: accuracy with a Wilson CI, κ and the % sent to human review.
crit: Your hand-computed κ for labeled_sample.csv comes out to 0.58 at two decimals, and you show po, pe and the 2×2 table.
git log --oneline shows the labels commit before the first commit with any judge output.
The report says who wrote the reference labels; if an assistant drafted them, it includes the log of each decision on your blind sample and the agreement with it.

Threshold and margin come only from the calibration split. The report includes the held-out set with n, Wilson CI and κ, and your κ matches cohen_kappa in agenteval/metrics.py or sklearn.metrics.cohen_kappa_score.
No case passes on the judge's confidence alone: the gray-zone cases show up in a human review list, counted.
Your 2 code checks catch at least one defect you seeded yourself, marked as seeded.
m17.deliver: κ computed by hand + a 20-case golden set with a rubric and labels written first + 2 code checks + a held-out report (accuracy with CI, κ and % sent to review).
m17.mut: Switch off a code guard. In a copy of agent-eval-jev, change the line "numbers_grounded": not unsupported, in agenteval/checks.py to "numbers_grounded": True,. Before running, write down what you expect from pytest -q, from python -m agenteval gate and from git diff --exit-code -- results reports after python -m agenteval evaluate. Run all three and report which one screams and which one doesn't. The one that stays quiet is a finding.

Labels were written first, but you report on the same group you tuned on.
Tuning on calibration and reporting on held-out with n, CI and κ.
On top of that, you measure the judge's flip rate with repeated runs and report it.

You only look at the final answer.
There are code checks, but no seeded defect puts them to the test.
Two code checks and seeded defects they catch, marked as seeded.
On top of that, an indirect injection case with a canary.
The judge decides everything.

m22.title: Judges that return probabilities — failure modes, stability and cascades
m22.mentor: A judge that returns probabilities doesn't tell you it got it right: it tells you how sure it claims to be. That's useful for routing, not for passing. Here you decide what happens when the judge goes down, you measure whether its verdict changes between identical runs, and you put a cheap judge in front of an expensive one without letting it block anything until you've measured it.
m22.kid: If the referee isn't sure, he doesn't make things up: he asks for the replay. And a new referee first watches a few games before you let him blow the whistle.
obj: Choose fail-closed, fail-open or fail-safe depending on how the judge is used.
Measure a judge's flip rate and declare it STABLE or UNSTABLE.
Design a judge cascade in shadow mode.
m22.pre: The agents module and the determinism module.
theory: Three failure policies for the same kind of judge: fail-closed for assertions (playwright-jev: unverified never passes), fail-open for triage (jev-ci-triage: unknown · unverified, no guessing) and fail-safe for selection (jev-test-impact: full suite).
Confidence is self-reported: in jev-ci-triage the same input came back with 0.69, 0.71, 0.78 and 0.84 against a 0.75 threshold. A case near the threshold can land on either side.
Flip rate: the share of decisions that change between identical runs. Pin the model, the temperature and the prompt version.
war-paradigm 01 runs the same input 3 times: with pins the verdict stays STABLE; without pins it's UNSTABLE and flips from approved to rejected.
Redact before sending: tokens, JWTs, emails, card numbers and personal paths are stripped from the text (jev-ci-triage/src/redact.ts).

Cascade (laya-server): a local CPU judge goes first; a state longer than 1500 characters goes to the cloud, a confidence below 0.8 escalates to Jev and a cloud error comes back with escalate: true for a person.

Shadow mode: responses are logged but block nothing. laya-server's README says it plainly: nobody has measured Laya's quality in Spanish yet, and that measurement comes before trusting it. That repo has no CI: only npm test runs the 7 policy cases.
hands: Write the “if the judge goes down, what happens” table for three of your own uses (an assertion, a triage, a selection), with the policy and why.
Run npm run demo:01 in war-paradigm and explain why the verdict is UNSTABLE without pins.
In laya-server, run npm test and add cases for a state of exactly 1500 characters and for a CASCADE_URL that's down. Propose the CI workflow it doesn't have today.
Measure a judge's flip rate with 5 repetitions over 20 cases.
Write a redactor (or reuse jev-ci-triage's) and test it with a log that contains a token, an email and a card number.
crit: Every use in the table has a policy (closed, open or safe) and a justification.
The flip rate comes with the number of cases and repetitions.
The two new laya-server cases pass with npm test.
The redactor removes the token, the email and the card number from the test log, and you show it.
m22.deliver: Failure-mode table + measured flip rate + new cascade cases + tested redactor.
m22.mut: Remove a pin (model, temperature or prompt version) and check whether the verdict becomes UNSTABLE.
m22.top: You propose the experiment that laya-server's README says is missing (a labeled set in Spanish), with the threshold written beforehand, and you don't turn on blocking until you have that number.

m23.title: AI-assisted QA II — the assistant designs, runs and audits; a person signs off
m23.mentor: I use assistants to design, run and audit tests faster, and the sign-off is mine. That only works with three things: hard rules in hooks and CI, not in prompts, because a prompt can be ignored; evidence someone else can rerun (command, hash and exit code); and a review that doesn't depend on a single pair of eyes. Whatever wasn't run gets said, and your own mistakes get published.
m23.kid: Telling the robot “please don't touch that” is a request; putting up a fence is a rule. And if a friend does the experiment for you, you write down every step so someone else can repeat it and get the same thing, and you say what you didn't get to. You're the one who signs.
obj: Explain, using the scientific-qa-evidence case, what the assistant did and what the person decided, citing AUTHORSHIP.md and the “How AI was used” section.
Run npm test for war-paradigm's experiment 03 and explain why the hook exits with 2 on a push to main and with 0 on a push to a branch.
Reproduce at 1b01c66~1 the hole a WAR mutation found in the hook, write the test that catches it and compare it with the fix in 1b01c66.
Deliver an audit operated by an assistant that someone else repeats with the same exit codes and hashes, with a blind double review and a “What was not executed” section.
m23.pre: The AI-assisted QA I module (hooks), the pipelines module, bash and git. Node 20 or newer and Python 3.9 or newer.
theory: The split: the assistant designs, runs and audits; the person chooses the questions, decides what counts as evidence and signs off. In scientific-qa-evidence, Codex was the main agent at first and Claude Code made the later changes; every commit names the agent in a Co-Authored-By trailer, and “Cristian Guerra chose the questions, froze the contracts, decided what counts as evidence and answers for every claim” (README, “How AI was used”).

Rules in code, not in prompts: “Hard rules live in code, not in prompts. Hooks, CI gates and reviews that can't be forgotten” (criguex profile, “How I work”). In war-paradigm/03, a Claude Code PreToolUse hook registered in .claude/settings.json reads the call as JSON and exits with exit 2 (it blocks and shows the assistant the reason) when the target is main or master.

The hook is also a guard, and it gets tested (the WAR thread): tests/hook.test.mjs attacks the hook with cases against real temporary git repos, on main and on a branch, with three JSON parsers (jq, node, sed): refspecs like HEAD:main, force flags, chained commands, git -C and a bare git push while on main. A real case: a WAR mutation found that git -c core.x=y push origin main and git --no-pager push origin main got through with exit 0; commit 1b01c66 fixed the hook and added tests that fail against the old hook. Six bypasses stay open on purpose and are pinned by tests titled “known limits: these get through” (exit 0): B=main; git push origin $B, G=push; git $G origin main, git -c alias.p=push p origin main, sh -c, bash -c and eval. A regex hook is a barrier against mistakes, not a sandbox; \git push origin main was trivial to close and is now blocked.

Context before prompt: experiment 03's vault ships 00 - READ FIRST, Golden rules, roles, test data and known defects, and tests/vault-links.test.mjs breaks the build if a link points to a note that doesn't exist, if frontmatter is missing or if a note is left orphaned.

Evidence = command + hash + exit code. scientific-qa-evidence publishes “a public record of every command, version, hash and exit code, including the errors found and fixed.” shasum -a 256 -c evidence/SHA256SUMS.txt checks that every curated file is the published one, and python verificar.py prints OK or FAIL for six checks plus a fingerprint to compare with someone else.

Traced agents and double review: on Oct 20, 2026 Codex ran 19 sessions, one main session and 18 subagents, each with its own role. docs/CODEX_WORK_LOG.md lists tool calls, commits and the SHA-256 of every session file; two blind judges (jd_tts_a, jd_tts_b) and a scoped fixer (tts_safety_fix) that applied their notes; and a “What was not executed” section: the “auto-fix” illustrations were never run, and the log says so.

Declare what isn't independent and publish your mistakes. The Oct 23 cloud rebuild was operated by an assistant under human direction, and its README puts it under Limits: “It is not independent.” Of the 8 findings in FINDINGS.md, numbers 1, 3 and 8 were defects in the study itself.

m19.title: Preregistration and reproducibility — thresholds before the data and the same fingerprint on another machine
m19.mentor: Before generating the test data, I put the hypotheses and thresholds in a commit. I include comparators that should fail, to check whether the tests tell apart the cases they're meant to. I run the verification on several machines, compare each round's verdicts and fingerprint, and keep ledgers of discrepancies and false positives. When a hypothesis fails, I publish it anyway: H14 failed, I didn't touch anything to fix it, and round 4 came out of that failure.
m19.kid: Before the game you write down on a piece of paper who's going to win, put it in a sealed envelope and, if you're wrong, you still tell everyone; if your cousin does the same math at his house and gets the same number, you know it wasn't luck.
obj: Write a preregistration with numbered hypotheses, numeric criteria, positive and negative controls, a comparator that must fail and limits, in a commit that comes before the data.
Run predictor-debugger's verify.py --saved on four saved environments (mac, war, guerra, linux) and get EEC9-09E0-F77D with verdicts equal ...: True.
Show that changing one byte of thresholds.json changes the fingerprint and makes the verifier exit with code 1.
Explain, with the repo's numbers, why H14 failed, why its threshold wasn't moved and what it opened up in round 4.
Compute a cluster bootstrap interval and explain why resampling steps makes it too narrow.
m19.pre: The modules on evaluating AI with a judge and on calibration (thresholds fixed beforehand, held-out, kappa), and the pipelines module (CI with a matrix). Git, basic Python and uv installed.
theory: Preregistration. predictor-debugger's DESIGN.md starts like this: “Written before any dataset, model or prediction exists”. Every later change is an amendment at the end, with a date, a reason and a commit, and none can be made after the test split has been evaluated. A real example: amendment 1 (Oct 24, before the data) added the P0f32 control and hypothesis H1b because the network was trained in float32 and D1 would have flagged it for rounding, not for physics.
What's being tested is the check, not the product. “A poor network is an acceptable result; a debugger that cannot tell the controls apart is a failure” (DESIGN.md §Question).

Positive and negative controls. P0 is the exact solver and must be accepted (H1). P3a adds a gradient of 5 % of ‖u‖ and breaks incompressibility: D1 must catch it (H2). P3b multiplies by 1.05 and injects energy: D2 must catch it (H3). P1 repeats the state and has no dynamics: D3 must catch it (H4). Each hypothesis pairs a control with the check that must scream.

Threshold fixed beforehand. τ = 10 × the maximum of P0 (and P0f32) on validation, with a floor of 1e-12, written once in thresholds.json with its hash. A step with NaN or infinity is always flagged: a NaN never passes.

Comparators that must fail. H14 required its cheap comparator (ΣD3) not to meet the same criterion. That's why it has three outcomes: PASS (the criterion holds and the comparator doesn't), NON-DISCRIMINATIVE (both hold) and FAIL (the criterion doesn't hold). In round 2, H8 passed but didn't tell G apart from D3: D3 also ranked that set.

A failed hypothesis, published. H14 asked for a mean ρ ≥ 0.7 with a lower CI ≥ 0.5 across all four networks. P2gbest got 0.635 [0.413; 0.795] and ΣD3 held on three out of four. Result: FAIL, “Nothing was changed to fix it.” Round 4 preregistered a new idea, H17 (carry the direction of the defect instead of adding up sizes), which passed on all four networks with means from 0.987 to 0.997.

Fingerprint. verify.py builds a sorted JSON with the numpy version, the solver's hash, the hash of every pd/*.py, the hash of thresholds.json, the input hashes and a summary of the verdicts, takes its SHA-256 and keeps 12 characters: EEC9-09E0-F77D. If one byte of any of those things changes, the fingerprint changes.

Several machines, without picking the convenient one. Mac, WAR and GUERRA, plus Linux in GitHub's CI and in WSL2, gave the same fingerprints. Round 1 discrepancy ledger: 0 entries. False-positive ledger: 126 entries, all D2 on P0/P0f32 in the out-of-distribution split, and all still open. And the written limit: “All three machines are mine, so this is not an independent reproduction.”

Bit-identical is not verdict-identical. No file regenerated on WAR, GUERRA or Linux came out bit-for-bit equal to the Mac's; the biggest difference was 8.9e-16. That's why the Mac's files are the canonical ones and what gets compared is verdicts and fingerprints.

Cluster bootstrap. In round2/evaluate.py, cluster_bootstrap resamples whole trajectories (each one carries all its steps), 2,000 replicates with the fixed seed 20261024, and reports the 2.5 and 97.5 percentiles. Steps from the same trajectory aren't independent: resampling them one by one would give a narrower interval than the data allows.

uv — Python environments with a lockfile

hands:
Step 1 · Level (a), saved verdicts: minutes, no data. You need git and uv; uv run --locked uses Python 3.9 and numpy 1.26.4 from uv.lock.

Step 5 · The cluster bootstrap. Read cluster_bootstrap in round2/evaluate.py. Then write a synthetic example (10 trajectories of 10 highly correlated steps) and compare the CI from resampling steps with the CI from resampling trajectories, using the same seed.

Verifiable exercise · Preregister your own QA experiment. For example: “my judge catches at least 90 % of the seeded false greens” or “my suite kills at least 5 of 6 mutants.” In a repo of your own: (1) PREREGISTRO.md with the question, at least 3 numbered hypotheses with a numeric criterion, a control that must pass, one that must fail, a comparator that must fail and limits; (2) the thresholds in thresholds.json; (3) commit; (4) only then, generate data and run; (5) a huella.py that prints a fingerprint over code, thresholds, inputs and verdicts; (6) a workflow with a two-OS matrix that does grep -q "fingerprint: XXXX-XXXX-XXXX", like predictor-debugger's .github/workflows/verify.yml; (7) a cluster bootstrap CI with the seed and number of replicates written down.
crit: git log --reverse --format="%h %ad %s" --date=iso shows the commit with PREREGISTRO.md and thresholds.json before the first data or results file.
git log -p -- thresholds.json shows no changes after the first run; if there were amendments, each one has a date, a reason and a commit and comes before the test evaluation.
Every hypothesis has its PASS or FAIL verdict published with the number that decides it; the ones that fail stay in the report.
In the run, the positive control passes and the negative control gets flagged; the comparator is reported even if it holds.
The CI job prints the same fingerprint on both operating systems and fails if you change one byte of thresholds.json (you show it with a test commit and its red job).
The CI resamples clusters, not rows, and the report states the seed and replicates.
The README has “Limits” and “What would contradict me”.

m19.mut: In a copy of the repo, change one byte of thresholds.json that isn't a number (for example a letter in the hostname) and run uv run --locked verify.py --saved mac; echo "exit=$?". The five verdicts stay at PASS and verdicts equal stays True, but changed thresholds.json shows up, the fingerprint is no longer EEC9-09E0-F77D and you get exit=1. Then restore the file and raise the D1 threshold to 1.0: H2 turns into 0/400 ... FAIL and verdicts equal into False. If your own verifier doesn't scream in either case, it's asleep: publish that.

m32.title: Requirements QA — reviewing the spec before building
m32.mentor: A product owner brought in a spec for a weekly competitor-monitoring tool. Before writing a single line of code, I reviewed it: I read every page, added up every number and wrote down everything that didn't add up or was missing. That produced 19 issues, 7 questions for the owner and a phased plan instead of a build. Every issue was fixed with a question on paper, before anyone spent weeks building the wrong thing. A preregistration is also a spec: review it with this same checklist.
m32.kid: Before you bake a cake you read the whole recipe, and if one page says 3 eggs and another says 2, you ask before you turn on the oven.
obj: Apply the 26-point checklist to a spec and log every finding with its five fields.
Recompute a spec's figures with a script that exits with a non-zero code as long as a contradiction remains.
Rate severity (Blocker, High, Medium) using the case's scale and state that it's judgment, not measurement.
Turn the blockers into numbered questions and the build into phases with gates.
Test the reviewer: measure how many seeded errors your own script catches.
m32.pre: The test design module (boundary values, decision tables) and the modules on evaluating AI with a judge and on calibration, to understand F13. Basic Python.
theory: First, where the spec came from. If it was put together from another company's screenshot or demo, its numbers are examples, not requirements. In the case study, that single observation explains a good chunk of findings F01 to F10.

The six-step process (README.es.md §Cómo funciona): read once to understand the intent; recompute every number; challenge the “facts” (costs and latencies); trace every definition back to its source; rate severity; decide with numbered questions and a phased plan.
Three families of problems. 7 numbers that don't add up, 3 costs or latencies presented as facts and 9 things nobody defined: 19 findings, 4 of them blockers.

Numbers that don't add up. F06: the “weekly” window (Aug 20 – Sep 27) lasts 38 days. F05: 14 competitors are announced, 12 are listed (they add up to 1,517 of 2,070 signals) and the graph draws 7. F04: escalations to a person are 31, 2 and 2 on the same screen, and the summary promises 3 actions and shows 2.

Acceptance tests that test nothing (F10): requiring a weekly spend of $0.2087 ± $0.01, 67 % noise and a P50 between 200 and 250 ms just copies someone else's week of data. With real data those tests fail even if the system works, or pass even if it doesn't. The proposal: 10 fixed signals that check the JSON contract and the escalation rules.

Thresholds on uncalibrated probabilities (F13): a 0.85 on the model's output means nothing without a labeled set. The proposal was a calibration phase in which the owner labels about 100 signals. It's the same problem as in the judge calibration module.

Severity. Blocker: that part can't be built or tested until someone answers. High: if it's built this way, it shows a wrong number, does the wrong thing, costs more or carries legal risk. Medium: it's confusing, but it doesn't stop anything. It's the reviewer's judgment, not a measurement, and the repo says so in its Limits.

The math, in code. check_numbers.py recomputes F01 to F08 with the spec's own figures, with no dependencies. ✗ is a contradiction, ! a number that may be true but isn't explained, and the script exits with code 1 as long as any of them remains.
The checklist. docs/checklist.es.md: 26 points in blocks 0 to 6, each tagged with the finding that made it necessary. You paste it into the ticket before anyone writes code.

Deciding. The review ended in a phased plan with gates: P0 with no code and 7 questions for the owner; P1 a 1–2 day MVP whose gate is the 10-fixed-signals test; P2 calibrate (“measured precision, not assumed”); P3 a UI only if P2 proves value; P4 scale.

Step 2 · Read the script. Open check_numbers.py and note which constant feeds each check (for example, WINDOW → F06, PER_COMPETITOR and GRAPH_NODES → F05). Every constant is a figure copied from the spec.

Step 3 · From the checklist to the finding. With docs/checklist.es.md and docs/findings.es.md open, for each of the 26 points find the finding in brackets and read its “How it was detected”. The four points that have no finding (the first one in block 0 and the three in block 6) close the review: write down what each one would prevent.
Step 4 · From the finding to the question. Take the 4 blockers (F11, F12, F16, F18) and rewrite each one as a question the owner can answer in minutes. Compare them with the 7 questions of phase P0.

Verifiable exercise · Review a real spec before anyone builds it. It can be a user story with acceptance criteria from your job (anonymized), a public API's documentation or the preregistration from your previous module. Deliver: (1) findings.md with at least 8 findings, each with what it said, why it's a problem, how it was detected, severity and decision or question, and the checklist line that covers it; (2) your own check_numbers.py with at least 4 checks that recompute figures from that spec and exit with 1 if a contradiction remains; (3) a corrected copy of the figures that makes the script exit with 0 (positive control) and at least 3 mutants, each with a single error seeded in a different check (negative controls); (4) the numbered questions for the owner and a phased plan with its gates.
crit: Your check_numbers.py exits with 1 on the original figures and with 0 on the corrected copy.
Every seeded mutant makes the script exit with 1; you report your script's kill rate and, if any survives, you leave it in plain sight.
Every finding has all five fields and points to a checklist line.
Every blocker ended up as a numbered question that can be answered in minutes.
The plan has phases with gates, the first phase has zero code, and git log shows no product code before the review was closed.
Company, people and product names are anonymized, as in the case study.

Now the dangerous mutant: restore it and change WEEK_SPEND to 0.40. F08 comes out ✓ even though a $0.40 spend is still unexplained: the check only flags when the spend matches “classifier input only”. That mutant survives. Write the check that would kill it and publish it as a finding against the reviewer.
